sections.heading: Asking you to make sin hateful to me
sections.text: Lord Jesus, give me a repentance that goes deeper than feeling bad after I have done wrong. Help me see sin for what it is, not as a small mistake or a private weakness, but as something that turns my heart away from you. Make me quick to run from it when it comes near. Guard my loves, my desires, and my choices, so that my heart belongs to you and not to anything that competes with you.
theological_themes: Repentance is not mere regret but a Spirit-worked turning from sin to Christ.
Sin must be resisted early, not entertained until it becomes action.
Christ alone deserves the undivided allegiance of the heart.

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers to reject evil sincerely and cling to what is good. This supports the prayer’s request for a deeper hatred of sin rather than a casual attitude toward it.
Paul tells Timothy to flee sinful desires and pursue righteousness with a clean heart. The passage fits the prayer’s plea to run from sin quickly and guard the heart for God.

sections.heading: Trusting you deeply enough to lose myself in you
sections.text: Teach me to trust you more deeply. Free me from the need to protect my own little kingdom. Let me lose the false version of myself that I cling to, so that I can find my true life in you. Be the solid ground under my feet, the rest my soul comes home to, and the source of every breath and every good desire in me.
theological_themes: True life is found not in self-preservation but in belonging to Christ.
Christ is the believer’s rest and foundation.
Dependence on Christ is not loss but life.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that saving one’s life by self-rule leads to loss, while losing one’s life for him is the path to true life. This directly grounds the prayer’s language of losing the self in order to be found in Christ.
Jesus invites the weary to come to him for rest under his gentle lordship. That supports the prayer’s request to find deep rest in him rather than in control, achievement, or self-protection.

sections.heading: Knowing you as Savior, Master, Lord, and King
sections.text: Let me know you more truly, Jesus—not just know correct things about you, but know you yourself. Show me again that you are my Savior, the one who rescues me; my Master, the one I gladly learn from; my Lord, the one I obey; and my King, the one who has every right to rule me. Keep me from wanting your comfort while resisting your authority.
theological_themes: Christ is not divided: he is Savior and Lord together.
Knowing Christ involves personal trust, obedience, and worship.
Christian discipleship includes gladly receiving Christ’s rule.

scripture_references.connection: Paul counts everything as loss compared with knowing Christ and sharing in the life that comes from him. The passage supports the prayer’s desire for a deeper, personal knowledge of Jesus rather than merely external religion.
Jesus accepts the titles Teacher and Lord and then shows that his disciples should follow his example. This connects Christ’s identity as Master and Lord with obedient, humble discipleship.

sections.heading: Going deeper in prayer and in your Word
sections.text: Give me more life and honesty in secret prayer. Keep me from praying only with my lips while my heart wanders somewhere else. Open your Word to me so that I taste its goodness, trust its truth, and hold on to it when my feelings are weak. Make Scripture more than information to me; use it to steady me, correct me, feed me, and draw me closer to you.
theological_themes: Private prayer is a place of real communion with God, not religious performance.
Scripture is God’s trustworthy Word and spiritual nourishment for the believer.
The believer needs grace to receive, love, and hold fast to biblical truth.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist asks God to open his eyes to behold the wonders of God’s law. This supports the prayer’s dependence on God for delight, understanding, and spiritual benefit from Scripture.
Paul calls believers to let the word of Christ dwell richly among them. The prayer echoes that desire for Scripture to take deep root and shape the inner life.

sections.heading: Becoming holy in a way that depends on you
sections.text: Make me holy in what I say, what I think, and what I do. But do not let me settle for a cleaned-up life that is disconnected from you. I do not want a thin layer of respectability over an unchanged heart. Join my obedience to love for you. Let every real virtue in me come from your life at work in me, not from pride, fear, or the need to look good.
theological_themes: Holiness reaches speech, thought, and action, not only outward behavior.
Moral change must be rooted in Christ, not self-righteousness or appearance.
Fruitfulness comes from abiding in Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that his disciples cannot bear fruit apart from abiding in him. This grounds the prayer’s refusal to seek moral virtue as something separate from Christ.
Peter calls believers to holiness in all their conduct because God is holy. This supports the prayer’s comprehensive concern for holiness in speech, thought, and action.

sections.heading: Letting you dig deep and make my life fruitful
sections.text: Lord, dig deep in me like a farmer breaking up hard ground. Do not only smooth the surface; turn over what is buried, break what is compacted, and make room for grace to take root. Grow your life in me until people see more of you and less of my self-centeredness. Let the beauty and fruitfulness of Christ show in me like a field ready for harvest.
theological_themes: God’s sanctifying work often goes beneath the surface and exposes what must be changed.
Grace is meant to take deep root and produce visible fruit.
The goal of transformation is that Christ would be seen and honored in the believer.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus describes the Father as the vinedresser who tends the branches so that they bear more fruit. The passage supports the prayer’s agricultural image of God’s deep cultivating work in the believer.
Paul describes the fruit produced by the Spirit in a believer’s life. This illuminates the prayer’s longing for grace to become visible in Christlike character.

sections.heading: Owning that everything good in me comes from you
sections.text: I have no true Master but you. Your will is the only law that can lead me into life. You are my deepest delight. Anything I have is a gift from your hand. Anything good in my life is good because you have blessed it. Any peace I know is peace you have given. I am not self-made. I am what you make me. I have what you give me. I can only become beautiful with the beauty your grace puts on me.
theological_themes: The believer’s life, possessions, goodness, and peace are received from God, not self-generated.
Christ’s lordship claims the whole person.
Grace is the source of all spiritual beauty and fruitfulness.

scripture_references.connection: Paul reminds believers that whatever they have has been received, leaving no room for boasting. This strongly supports the prayer’s confession that every good thing comes from God.
James teaches that every good and perfect gift comes from God. The passage fits the prayer’s dependence on God for every blessing, possession, and good.

sections.heading: Hollow me out, then fill me with living water
sections.text: So, Lord Jesus, go as deep as you need to go. Dig out what is false, proud, stubborn, and dead in me. Then fill the empty places with your own life until I overflow. Let living water rise in me—not for my credit, but because you are generous, and because a dry heart like mine can only live when you fill it.
theological_themes: Repentance and sanctification involve God exposing and removing what is dead or false in the heart.
Christ gives living water to the spiritually thirsty.
The believer depends on Christ not only for forgiveness but for ongoing life and renewal.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus invites the thirsty to come to him and speaks of living water connected with the Spirit’s work. This directly supports the prayer’s final request to be filled to overflowing with divine life.
The psalmist asks God to search him, expose what is grievous, and lead him in the everlasting way. This supports the prayer’s willingness for God to dig deeply and remove what does not belong.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s plea for a “horror of sin” and “dread of its approach” is intentionally severe. I preserved that moral seriousness while expressing it as hatred of sin and quick flight from it, rather than as a psychologically vague fearfulness.

The line about not seeking moral virtue apart from Christ could be misunderstood as rejecting ordinary moral responsibility. I rendered it as rejecting self-righteous or Christless respectability, while still praying for real holiness in speech, thought, and action.
significant_interpretive_choices: I kept the address to “Lord Jesus” throughout because the original prayer is explicitly addressed to Christ, even though some supporting texts speak of the Father’s cultivating work or the Spirit’s fruit. This preserves the Christ-centered direction of the original.

I interpreted the agricultural images of ploughing, roots, harvest, and fruitfulness as God’s deep sanctifying work that produces visible Christlike character, rather than as a request for outward ministry success.

I rendered “Quarry me deep” as God digging out what is false and dead, then filling the emptiness with living water. This keeps the original’s concrete excavation image while making its spiritual meaning clear for a modern reader.
